images.title: Average is not everyone
images.purpose: Show that a higher average for one group does not mean every member is taller than every member of the other group.
images.composition: Two short dot plot rows one above the other over one shared numbered scale, with a mean marker under each row and one highlighted dot; wide white space around.
exact_structure: One numbered grey (#6B7280) scale at the bottom from 130 to 155 with small ticks every 1 cm and numbers at 130, 135, 140, 145, 150 and 155; above it two thin grey row lines, one above the other, both aligned to this scale.
Upper row line, labelled Girls aged 11 at its left end: exactly 5 teal (#0072B2) dots at 132, 135, 138, 140 and 145.
Lower row line, labelled Girls aged 13 at its left end: exactly 5 amber (#E69F00) dots at 140, 144, 147, 150 and 154.
The teal dot at 145 is ringed in reddish purple (#CC79A7) because it is taller than the amber dots at 140 and 144.
A small grey (#6B7280) triangle under each row marks its mean: 138 for the upper row, 147 for the lower row, labelled mean 138 and mean 147.
Arithmetic check for the reviewer only, NOT drawn in the frame: 132 + 135 + 138 + 140 + 145 = 690, 690 ÷ 5 = 138; 140 + 144 + 147 + 150 + 154 = 735, 735 ÷ 5 = 147.
rejection: a row with other than 5 dots
the ringed dot not at 145 in the upper row
images.takeaway: A higher average describes the group, not every member of it.
images.description: Two dot plots of five heights each, means 138 and 147, with one 11 year old at 145 taller than two 13 year olds.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students to find the dots that break the claim that every 13 year old is taller.

image_decisions.why: Shows why a table of averages cannot justify a claim about every individual.
